title: Tilda and the Lost Mouse
markdown:
Whoooo knows the quiet magic held within the Misty Crags, especially when the moon hangs like a pearl in the sky? It is known among the forest folk that these ancient stones have seen countless stories unfold. Tucked between the mossy roots of a pine that reached for the stars lived Tilda, a young witch whose spells were as gentle as a butterfly's wing. Her cottage, a cozy haven, always hummed with the comforting scent of lavender and simmering herbs, and her friendly mountain lantern cast a honey-gold glow that made the shadows dance away, leaving only warmth and safety.

One evening, as Tilda stirred a pot of sleepy-time stew, smelling of moonlight and dreams, she heard a tiny, frantic scrabbling. It wasn't the familiar rustle of a beetle or the soft thump of a dropped spell book. This was a small, worried sound, like a little leaf caught in a sudden, blustery sigh of wind.

“Whoooo is that?” Tilda whispered, her voice like the rustle of dry leaves. She settled down like a falling leaf and peered under her armchair, its cushions soft and worn. There, quivering like a dewdrop on a spider’s web, was a little mouse. He was so small his whiskers seemed as long as his body, and his fur was the colour of a dusty acorn, blending perfectly with the cottage floor. He looked quite, quite lost, his tiny paws tucked underneath him as if he were trying to melt into the rug.

Tilda knelt down, her starry robe pooling around her like a spilled midnight sky. “Oh, you poor little thing,” she said, her voice as soft as the down of a young owl. “You’ve strayed from your family, haven’t you? It’s a big, wide world for such a little creature.”

The mouse gave a tiny, shaky squeak, a sound barely audible above the gentle bubbling of Tilda’s stew.

“Don’t you worry,” Tilda assured him, her eyes sparkling like tiny constellations. “We’ll get you home. What’s your name, little one?”

He blinked his bead-like eyes, which seemed to hold a universe of worry. “Pipkin,” he squeaked, his voice a whisper of a rustle, like leaves skittering across a path.

Tilda smiled. “Pipkin. That’s a very nice name. And Pipkin, I’m Tilda. I live right here in the Misty Crags. We can help you find your way. My cottage is safe, and so are the woods outside, especially with my lantern.”

Pipkin trembled a little more, his whole body a tiny quake. The world outside Tilda’s warm cottage seemed very big and very dark, and he was sure he’d never find his way back.

“It’s alright,” Tilda said, scooping him up very gently, her hands as soft as moss. She held him for a moment, feeling his tiny heart beat like a hummingbird’s wings against her palm. “My mountain lantern will light our way. It knows all the paths, you see. It remembers the way the moonbeams fall on the forest floor.” Pipkin settled a little, finding the warmth of Tilda’s hand and the steady glow of the lantern quite comforting. It was much warmer and safer than he had imagined.

Tilda carefully placed Pipkin into a soft, moss-lined pouch she wore around her neck. The moss was gathered from the shadiest parts of the Crags, and it felt like sleeping on a cloud. Pipkin’s little nose poked out, and he seemed to feel much braver there, safe and sound, peeking out at the room. He could see Tilda’s friendly face and the familiar glow of her many little jars filled with sparkling dust and dried flowers. She picked up her mountain lantern, which pulsed with a gentle, steady light, brighter than any star, and filled the room with a warm, inviting glow. “Ready, Pipkin?” she asked, her voice full of cheerful anticipation.

Pipkin gave a determined little nod, his whiskers twitching with a touch of bravery.

And so, Tilda and Pipkin stepped out into the cool, crisp night air. The whispering pines stood tall and silent, their needles rustling softly, sharing secrets with the wind that danced through their branches. The moon, a sliver of pearly light, hung high above, watching over the sleepy mountains like a gentle eye. Tilda’s lantern bobbed along, a friendly little sun in the dimness, casting dancing shadows that looked like playful sprites on the forest floor, making the familiar path seem like a magical adventure.

They hadn’t gone far, not even past the first cluster of sleepy bluebells, when they heard a peculiar, humming sound. It was like a bumblebee wearing spectacles, a gentle buzz mixed with the rustle of many, many papers being shuffled. Around a bend in the path, where the moonlight dappled the ground, they saw him. It was Barnaby Bright, the wizard who lived on the highest peak, known throughout the Misty Crags for his kindness and his… rather enthusiastic collection of maps. Barnaby had maps of everything: maps of the clouds shaped like animals, maps of lost socks that vanished from the laundry, maps of the taste of sunshine on a summer’s day.

Barnaby squinted at them, his long, star-dusted beard tickling his chin and making him look like a benevolent, fluffy cloud. “Well, hello there, Tilda!” he boomed, his voice like pebbles rolling down a gentle slope. “And who is this little fellow peeking out from your pouch?”

“This is Pipkin, Barnaby,” Tilda said, her voice bright and clear. “He’s lost his way home, and I’m helping him find his cozy burrow.”

“Lost, you say?” Barnaby tutted, a sound of deep concern. He began to rummage through his enormous, bulging satchel, pulling out a rolled-up scroll. “Hmm, this is most unfortunate. Let me see. I have a map here of all the mouse-holes in the Crags. Ah, yes!” He unfurled it with a flourish. It looked very much like all his other maps, covered in squiggly lines and tiny, illegible notes that seemed to dance on the parchment. “Pipkin, my dear boy, where abouts do you live?”

Pipkin, peeking from Tilda’s pouch, squeaked, “Near the big, twisty oak tree by the Sparkle Stream. It has the best acorns!”

Barnaby tapped his chin with a long, bony finger. “Sparkle Stream… twisty oak… that sounds familiar. Ah! This map says… no, wait. Is that a cloud or a badger’s burrow? Oh dear, this one seems to be a map of my breakfast yesterday. I distinctly remember a rather good blueberry muffin. Never mind!” He pulled out another, even larger map, this one unfurling to reveal a dizzying array of lines. “This one is definitely it! See, Tilda? It shows a little red X right… here!” He pointed to a spot that looked suspiciously like a smudge of ink, or perhaps a very surprised ladybug.

Tilda peered at it, her brow furrowed slightly. It looked rather like a very fluffy sheep, or perhaps a particularly bumpy cloud that had decided to take a nap on the map. “Are you sure, Barnaby?” she asked gently. “It looks a little bit like a picture of your favourite teacup, the one with the little bluebirds on it.”

Barnaby blinked, his eyes widening behind his spectacles. “Does it? Good heavens, it might! I do have a rather lovely teacup. Perhaps this is a map of my teacup collection. So many maps, you see, they all start to look alike after a while. Whoooo could blame a wizard for getting them mixed up? It’s like trying to tell one snowflake from another!” He chuckled, a sound like pebbles rolling down a hill, a warm and friendly sound.

Pipkin wriggled slightly in the pouch. He was starting to feel a little more worried again. Barnaby’s maps were interesting to look at, with all their swirls and dots, but they didn’t seem to be pointing him towards his warm bed or his mama.

Tilda, ever patient and observant, looked around. The air here smelled faintly of damp earth and sweet clover, a familiar scent that always made her feel calm. Her lantern’s light played on the bark of the trees, highlighting patterns that looked like sleepy faces. And then she noticed something, or rather, she heard something. “Barnaby,” she said gently, “Pipkin said his home is near the Sparkle Stream. Do you hear that?”

They both stopped and listened. And there it was, a faint, tinkling sound, like tiny silver bells being shaken by the wind. It was the Sparkle Stream, much closer than Barnaby’s map suggested, its water bubbling merrily over smooth stones. And just beyond it, illuminated by Tilda’s steady lantern light, was a truly magnificent, twisty oak tree, its branches reaching out like welcoming arms.

“Oh my goodness!” Barnaby exclaimed, his eyes wide with surprise. “The Sparkle Stream! And the twisty oak! Why, Pipkin, my dear boy, your home is right over there!” He gestured with a flourish, nearly dropping his teacup map in his excitement. “It seems my map wasn’t quite… accurate. More of a suggestion, really.” He gave Tilda a sheepish grin, the stars in his beard twinkling. “Perhaps I should stick to mapping my sock drawer. At least I know where all my socks are, even if they do like to hide in pairs!”

Pipkin wriggled with pure excitement, his little nose twitching wildly. He could see a tiny opening at the base of the twisty oak, snuggled amongst the roots like a secret doorway. It looked so cozy and familiar, exactly as he remembered it.

Tilda carefully took Pipkin out of her pouch. She knelt down so he could easily reach his home. “Here we are, Pipkin,” she said softly, her smile as warm as her hearth fire. “Your home. Safe and sound.”

Pipkin gave Tilda a grateful squeak and a tiny nudge of his head against her finger, a mouse’s way of saying thank you. Then, with a burst of happy energy, he scurried down towards the oak. He disappeared into the cozy opening, and a moment later, a few other tiny noses poked out from the darkness, followed by a flurry of happy squeaks. Pipkin was home, surrounded by his loving family.

Tilda watched them, a warm feeling spreading through her chest, like sunshine after a gentle rain. Barnaby Bright stood beside her, humming a cheerful tune and carefully rolling up his maps, perhaps to be sorted later. “Well, Tilda,” he said, his voice full of quiet wonder and a touch of awe. “That was a fine adventure for such a little mouse. And for a young witch with such a kind heart, too. You have a wonderful way with lost creatures.”

As the first blush of dawn painted the sky in soft shades of rose and gold, chasing away the last of the night’s indigo, Tilda and Barnaby turned back towards their homes. The whispering pines seemed to sigh contentedly, their rustling a soft lullaby to the waking world. The mountain lantern in Tilda’s hand cast a contented, honey-gold glow, reflecting the warmth of their good deed and the dawning of a new day. Whoooo could have guessed that a lost mouse and a wizard with too many maps would lead to such a sweet adventure, ending just as the sun began to peek over the highest peaks? The trees remembered this story well, the story of a kind young witch who helped a brave little mouse find his way home, and of a night of gentle magic in the Misty Crags.
characters: Tilda the young witch, a mouse
